stories.headline: MAP IT: DOJ illegal voting crackdown sweeps 17 states as razor-thin elections face scrutiny
stories.note: The Justice Department charged 64 noncitizens in 17 states with illegal voting and fake registrations in about five weeks, as it ramps up election-integrity enforcement before the midterms.
body: Federal prosecutors have charged 64 foreign nationals in 17 states over roughly the past five weeks with illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration and related crimes, according to Justice Department figures shared with Fox News Digital. The department says it has now charged 104 people with voting-fraud offenses since President Trump returned to office in 2025.

Minnesota tops the list with 11 defendants, followed by Pennsylvania with 10 and Texas with nine. Louisiana has five, and New Jersey, California and Florida have four each. The cases range from bogus registration forms to ballots cast in more than one election, and some defendants are already pleading guilty, including a Pennsylvania woman from the Philippines who admitted voting illegally in the 2024 presidential race.

DOJ pointed to Iowa's 2nd District in 2020, decided by just six votes, as proof that a handful of illegal ballots can swing a race. "Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen," a department spokesperson said. Other cases include a Haitian national in Philadelphia accused of filing eight registration applications and a Louisiana ex-mayoral candidate accused of registering a Jamaican national as a citizen.

In New Jersey, Republicans have highlighted about 6,600 people who said they weren't citizens but were mistakenly registered through the state's motor vehicle agency; Gov. Mikie Sherrill's administration says fewer than 400 of them voted and that it fixed the error. Officials have not shown that any of the DOJ cases changed an election result.

Why it matters: The crackdown backs up a core Republican argument that voter-roll safeguards need tightening, and it puts Democratic-run states like Minnesota and New Jersey on the defensive just weeks before the November midterms.

stories.headline: Trump says he'd 'love' to have Sen. John Fetterman as a Republican amid growing speculation
stories.note: Trump openly invited Democratic Sen. John Fetterman to switch parties, saying he'd "love" to have him and that Fetterman polls better as a Republican.
body: Asked by a reporter at Joint Base Andrews on Saturday whether he'd welcome Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman into the GOP, President Trump didn't hesitate. "I'd love to see it. I think he's great," he said, adding that Fetterman would have a hard time winning the Democratic nomination again.

Trump called Fetterman a solid person with great common sense and said he'd spoken with the senator's parents before. He also argued that a switch would help Fetterman politically, claiming polls show him doing better as a Republican than as a Democrat.

Fetterman has broken with his party on big issues like the Iran war and immigration. He has voted with Senate Democrats nearly 90% of the time since 2023, but that has dropped to just under 81% in the current Congress, according to Fox News Digital's earlier reporting.

The speculation has been building: Fetterman has reportedly used Republican fundraising platforms, is close friends with GOP Sen. Katie Britt, and recorded a video introducing Republican Sen. Dave McCormick at the Republican Midterm Convention. At a Texas event last month he even slipped and called himself a "lifelong Republican" before catching the mistake.

Why it matters: Even the possibility of a sitting Democratic senator crossing over shows how far some moderates have drifted from their party's left wing, and a switch would hand Republicans another Senate seat without an election.

stories.headline: NYC councilwoman blasts Mamdani over Italian Heritage Month post praising 'communist'
stories.note: Mayor Mamdani marked Italian Heritage Month by praising a far-left congressman with Communist Party ties, and Queens Councilwoman Vickie Paladino tore into him for it.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's Italian Heritage Month post on X drew a wave of criticism after he chose to honor Vito Marcantonio, a seven-term East Harlem congressman. Mamdani wrote that he'd keep fighting for Marcantonio's "vision of a government that works for all working people."

Marcantonio started out as a Republican but later served with the left-wing American Labor Party. His opposition to the Korean War and his legal work for the Communist Party drew FBI scrutiny, and the bureau kept files on him during the Cold War.

Queens Councilwoman Vickie Paladino called Marcantonio an obscure Italian-American communist and accused the mayor of pushing communist propaganda. "Of all the great men and women of Italian descent who've contributed to New York City and the United States, this is the idiot he picks," she wrote.

Paladino contrasted the post with her own family's story: her father fought Mussolini's forces in World War II, and her mother raised five children alone while working in a button factory. She said Italian-Americans were proud to learn English and wave the American flag. Mamdani's office didn't respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Why it matters: It's another flashpoint for Mamdani, the Democrats' highest-profile socialist, and gives Republicans fresh ammunition to tie the party to far-left politics heading into the midterms.

stories.headline: California faces unlikely tax revolt amid billions in illegal immigrant healthcare costs
stories.note: Newsom's plan to raise a health-plan tax to prop up Medi-Cal, which spent an estimated $12.4 billion on care for illegal immigrants last year, has doctors and insurers suing to stop it.
body: Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers are backing a redesigned tax on private health plans to keep billions flowing into Medi-Cal, California's Medicaid program, after federal rules under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act limited how states can use such taxes to draw federal matching money. If approved, the higher levy would start in 2027.

The program's costs have soared, and covering immigrants without legal status cost the state an estimated $12.4 billion in 2025, according to the Associated Press. Brian Blase of the right-leaning Paragon Health Institute said yes when asked whether that expansion created the need to raise taxes, and he estimated the plan would add about $400 a year to a family's insurance costs.

In an unusual alliance, the California Medical Association and the California Association of Health Plans are suing to block the tax. They argue it breaks Proposition 35, a voter-approved measure capping taxes on commercial health plans. "The state does not get to ignore that law simply because following the law is inconvenient," the medical association's CEO, Dustin Corcoran, said.

Insurers estimate premiums could rise by about $100 per person per year. Newsom's office says the tax is legal and expects to win in court, and state finance officials say they are submitting two versions to federal regulators, one of which conforms to the new federal law by shifting costs toward private plans.

Why it matters: The fight puts a price tag on California Democrats' decision to extend Medi-Cal to illegal immigrants, in a state already losing residents over the cost of living, and it lets Republicans argue that working families with private insurance will foot the bill.

stories.headline: Key American industry seeing blue-collar jobs boom as Trump's reshoring policies pay off
stories.note: A new White House economic report says 72,000 manufacturing jobs have been added in 2026, reversing a Biden-era slide, with factory pay up 7.9% since January 2025.
body: A new report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers, shared first with Fox News, says the U.S. has added 72,000 manufacturing jobs in 2026 alone, many in durable goods like metals and transportation equipment. The report says that reverses a trend in which about 200,000 factory jobs disappeared in the last two years of the Biden administration.

The council credits Trump's reshoring push and tariffs, along with the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which lets manufacturers immediately deduct 100% of the cost of new factories and equipment. Ohio-based Jergens used that provision to expand into Illinois, and North Carolina's Ketchie Inc. says it grew its workforce by 25% after buying new machinery once the law passed.

Jergens CEO Jack Schron said 83% of his workers are now taking overtime after the law ended taxes on overtime pay, calling it "a win-win-win" for workers, the company and the economy. The report also says manufacturing wages are up 7.9% since January 2025, which it calls nearly $2,500 more a year after inflation, and that 100,000 construction jobs have been added.

It points to big investments like Micron's memory-chip plants in Idaho, Virginia and New York and Apple's $600 billion commitment to U.S. chip production, and says total new investment in Trump's second term has hit $11 trillion. The article also notes voters remain worried about prices: a Fox News Poll found 61% call gas prices a major problem, and nearly two-thirds say the economy is worse under Trump.

Why it matters: Factory jobs and rising blue-collar paychecks give Republicans a concrete economic story to sell in the final weeks before the midterms, even as cost-of-living worries remain the biggest hurdle.

stories.headline: President talks 'Trump Ocean,' trades jokes with Tennessee crowd as Kid Rock kicks off sprawling rally
stories.note: Trump and Kid Rock fired up a Clarksville, Tennessee, crowd for Sen. Bill Hagerty and governor candidate Marsha Blackburn, touting a $6.6 billion investment and a big drop in Memphis crime.
body: President Trump held a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, on Saturday to campaign for Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty and gubernatorial candidate Marsha Blackburn ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms. Kid Rock opened the event, joking that if Trump walked across the Cumberland River, the headline would say he "refuses to swim."

Trump spent much of his speech on jobs, highlighting Korea Zinc's $6.6 billion project, which Tennessee officials call the largest single private investment in state history. It's expected to create 740 jobs and includes what Trump said will be the first new mineral smelter built in the U.S. since 1979. He also cited GM's $275 million investment at its Spring Hill plant and credited his tariffs for the wave of new factories.

On crime, Trump praised federal operations in Memphis, saying about 12,000 dangerous criminals had been removed, and the White House says murders and overall crime there have fallen roughly 36%. A White House fact sheet also cited an average $3,674 tax refund for Tennesseans in 2026.

There were lighter moments too. Trump floated renaming an ocean the "Trump Ocean" or "Ocean of the Americas," joked that the Strait of Hormuz could become the "Trump Strait," and called Iran's leaders "crazy" while describing heavy damage to their military. He closed with a plea to supporters: "Pretend. Just pretend that I'm running."

Why it matters: Trump is putting his own energy into turning out voters in GOP strongholds, pairing big-dollar investment news with a tough-on-crime message as Republicans try to hold the line in November.

stories.headline: Socialists set sights on the ground floor of government as GOP warns of bigger plan unfolding
stories.note: At least 65 Democratic Socialists-backed candidates are on state legislative ballots, and a GOP memo warns they're a farm team pushing the Democratic Party further left.
body: At least 65 candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America have made it to November ballots for state legislative seats in 24 states, according to a memo from the Republican State Leadership Committee obtained by Fox News Digital. The Brookings Institution puts the count even higher, at 76 or more.

The RSLC argues the statehouse races are a pipeline: local and state offices give these candidates experience, donors and organizing networks they can later use to run for Congress. The memo warns of "a clearly orchestrated long-term effort to build political power from the state-level up."

Several of the candidates have taken stances Republicans say will alienate swing voters. New York State Sen. Jabari Brisport's campaign site pledges to end policing and incarceration in the state, Wisconsin Rep. Ryan Clancy has stood by a statement that police work has "no dignity or value," and New Mexico Rep. Eleanor Chávez has called ICE fascist. Clancy told Fox News Digital his remarks were about officers who abused their power.

Others push government takeovers of utilities, like New York Assemblywoman Sarahana Shrestha's bill to acquire Central Hudson Gas & Electric, possibly through eminent domain. Shrestha said the ideas are popular with voters. A September Fox News poll found 55% of registered voters view the DSA unfavorably, though Brookings notes DSA-backed candidates hold only a tiny share of state legislative seats.

Why it matters: Republicans see a chance to tie mainstream Democrats to an unpopular socialist wing, especially after a Schumer-aligned super PAC committed millions to progressive Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.
